cards.q: What is the main limitation of mean–variance optimization?
pts: Weights are very sensitive to errors in expected returns μ — small changes cause large weight swings ('error maximization').
Covariance estimation error, especially in Σ⁻¹ when assets are highly correlated or N is large relative to T.
Result: extreme, concentrated, unstable portfolios.
Remedies: shrinkage (Ledoit–Wolf), Black–Litterman, constraints, robust optimization, risk-based allocation.
cards.pit: Chopra & Ziemba (1993): errors in means matter roughly an order of magnitude more than errors in variances.

cards.q: What changes when you add transaction costs to portfolio optimization?
pts: The objective adds a cost on trades, e.g. Σ cᵢ|wᵢ − wᵢ⁰| (proportional) or a quadratic market-impact term.
Current holdings w⁰ become an input — the optimum depends on where you start.
It creates a no-trade region: you move only partway toward the target.
Multi-period: trade gradually toward a moving target (Gârleanu–Pedersen).
cards.pit: Costs depend on the change in holdings, not on the target weights alone.

cards.q: Risk parity vs minimum variance portfolio?
pts: Risk contribution of asset i: RCᵢ = wᵢ(Σw)ᵢ; the contributions sum to portfolio variance wᵀΣw.
Risk parity: equal (or target) risk contributions across assets.
Minimum variance: minimize wᵀΣw; ignores how risk is distributed and often concentrates in low-volatility assets.
If all pairwise correlations are equal, risk parity = inverse-volatility weights.
cards.pit: Equal risk contributions do not mean equal weights or minimum variance.

cards.q: What is Black–Litterman designed to address?
pts: Start from equilibrium implied returns π = δΣw_mkt (reverse optimization).
Combine with investor views Pμ = q + ε, ε ~ N(0, Ω), via Bayesian updating.
The posterior returns are more stable and give diversified portfolios that tilt toward views in proportion to confidence.
cards.pit: Results depend on calibrating τ, Ω and δ.

pts: Active return = r_portfolio − r_benchmark.
Tracking error = standard deviation of active returns (annualize by × √periods per year).
Information ratio = mean active return / tracking error.
cards.pit: TE is symmetric — it measures active volatility, not downside risk or expected underperformance.

pts: VaR_α: the α-quantile of the loss distribution.
ES / CVaR_α: the expected loss in the worst (1 − α) tail, i.e. beyond VaR (defined via an integral of quantiles for general distributions).
ES is coherent (subadditive) while VaR is not; ES can be optimized as an LP (Rockafellar–Uryasev).
cards.pit: Watch the sign convention (loss vs return) and the large estimation error in the tail.

cards.q: Why is Monte Carlo useful for multi-period asset allocation?
pts: Simulate joint return paths from an explicit stochastic model (e.g. regime-switching, block bootstrap).
Apply each dynamic policy along every path, including rebalancing and cash flows.
Compare the distributions: terminal wealth, probability of reaching the goal, drawdowns, shortfall.
cards.pit: Randomly generating portfolio weights is not the same as simulating return paths and evaluating a policy.

cards.q: What is robust optimization trying to protect against?
pts: Inputs (e.g. μ) are treated as lying in an uncertainty set U rather than at a single point estimate.
Optimize the worst case: max_w min_{μ∈U} (wᵀμ − λ wᵀΣw).
Ellipsoidal U around μ̂ ⇒ the worst case is wᵀμ̂ − κ‖Σ_μ^{1/2} w‖, a penalty term that makes it an SOCP.
cards.pit: A too-large uncertainty set is overly conservative; calibrating κ matters.
